statement: The numbers 1 to 9 are written in a row. You may swap any two neighbours as often as you like. Can the row ever end up exactly reversed after an odd number of swaps?

choices.misconception: I counted the nine numbers and assumed the swap count would match them.
I guessed an odd number near the right size without checking what each swap does to the ordering.

choices.text: No, because reversing needs an even number of swaps
No, because the row can never be reversed at all
choices.misconception: I concluded that an impossible parity meant the reversal itself was impossible, rather than just the odd count.

choices.text: Only if the middle number stays put
choices.misconception: I noticed the middle number does not move and treated that as the whole constraint.

hints: Count the pairs that are in the wrong order.
Each neighbour swap changes the number of out-of-order pairs by exactly one, so that count's parity flips every move. Compare the start and the target.
Reversing 1 to 9 puts all 36 pairs out of order, and 36 is even, so the number of single swaps must be even too.

solutions.reliable: Count inversions: pairs that appear in the wrong order. A swap of neighbours changes that count by exactly one, so its parity alternates with every move. The reversed row has 9 x 8 / 2 = 36 inversions, an even number, so only an even number of swaps can reach it. The transferable idea: find a quantity whose parity every move must flip, then compare the two ends.
solutions.elegant: 36 is even, so the answer is settled before any swapping is attempted.

whyOnTest: Parity invariants turn an impossible search into a one-line argument, and the 5-point block relies on them most years.
